Six months after submission a reviewer asks about Table 2, and you need the same
numbers from the same code. Data and code are the easy part. The packages have
moved in the meantime, because the server's library changes whenever someone
updates it, and nothing tells the projects that use it.

So each study keeps its own library, in its own directory, with every version
written down in a lockfile. [Start here](start-here.html) covers `setup()`, which
builds all of that once. This page is about living with it afterward: adding a
package, updating one, answering a revision, and fixing what goes wrong.

## What setup leaves in the study

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `renv.lock` | The record: every package's version, and each family member's commit |
| `DESCRIPTION` | The packages the study declares. A shared file, written by `setup()` and `study_need()` |
| `.Rprofile` | Starts renv when the project opens |
| `renv/settings.json` | The study's renv settings, the shared cache setting among them |
| `renv/library/` | The installed packages |

renv runs in explicit mode in our studies. The lockfile records what
`DESCRIPTION` declares, not whatever a script happens to mention, so a stale
template copy can never put a package into it. The other side of that bargain is
that a package you install with plain `install.packages()` is not recorded until
it is declared.

The library is shared too. `setup()` turns off renv's per-user cache for the
study, so the library holds real copies a teammate can read rather than links
into your home directory.

## Adding a package

For a package from the configured repositories, run this in the open project. It
installs the package, declares it and records it:

```r
hvtiRutilities::study_need("cmprsk")
```

A package from GitHub takes three steps:

```r
renv::install("org/repo")
hvtiRutilities::study_declare("repo")
renv::snapshot()
```

Run these in the console and keep them out of your jobs. Re-running a job should
never install anything or change its environment.

## Updating packages

An update is a decision about one study, so make it on purpose and record it.
For one package:

```r
renv::update("name")
renv::snapshot()
```

For the family, from a fresh session in the project, before anything attaches a
member:

```r
hvtiR::update()
renv::snapshot()
```

To see whether the library and the lockfile agree, use `renv::status()`.

## Bringing an active study on

The command is the one [Start here](start-here.html) gives, with `adopt = TRUE`.
Two courtesies come first on a study other people are working in. If it already
has a `renv.lock`, ask its owner before you run `setup()`. And warn the team,
because `setup()` changes the library their sessions load from; they should close
those sessions first.

A lockfile the study already has is kept. `setup()` restores the locked versions,
declares every package the lockfile recorded and installs only what is missing.
Do not run `renv::init()` on such a study, which starts its library over.

## Answering a revision

Open the project, on the R version the lockfile records, then rebuild the library
the study was submitted with and check it:

```r
renv::restore()
renv::status()
```

Then render the job as usual. If you need `setup()` on a study in revision, pass
`upgrade = FALSE`, so that a package the install would move stops the run.

⚠️ **`hvtiR::status()` does not check the lockfile.** It compares what is installed
with GitHub `main`, so a study held on its submitted versions is expected to show
members as `stale`. That is the lockfile doing its job. `renv::status()` is the
check that matters here, and running `hvtiR::update()` to clear the report would
move the very versions you are protecting.

## How the family is pinned

The family installs from GitHub `main`, so two people installing a week apart can
land on different commits under one version number. The lockfile is what fixes
that, because pak records the commit it installed from and renv reads that field:

```json
"hvtiPlotR": {
  "Package": "hvtiPlotR",
  "Version": "2.8.6",
  "RemoteUsername": "ehrlinger",
  "RemoteRepo": "hvtiPlotR",
  "RemoteSha": "a4f3c9d8..."
}
```

`renv::restore()` then brings each member back at that commit, with no install
steps of your own.

## Common problems

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| `setup()` stops before installing and prints a command | You ran it inside the project. Close the project, then run a command with the same arguments from outside it |
| "Could not solve package dependencies" | Run `hvtiR::doctor()`. It lists the repositories R uses, warns on a dated snapshot and names any version floor they cannot meet |
| `renv::restore()` fails on a package that is not on CRAN | Look for `RemoteRepo` in `renv.lock`. A package pinned on GitHub may need your own `GITHUB_PAT` |
| An install fails reading a package in someone's home directory | The library holds links into a per-user cache. Rerun `setup()` for the study: it turns the cache off and replaces the links with real copies |
| A package is installed but not in `renv.lock` | It is not declared. `hvtiRutilities::study_need("name")` declares and records it |
| `renv.lock` is behind the library | `renv::status()` shows the drift, and `renv::snapshot()` records it once you have checked that it is what you meant |
| A teammate's session errors just after setup | They had the project open while the library changed. Restart the session |
